events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Sam proposes Sam, Theo. Proposing myself and Theo for a balanced first mission. Neither of us has a track record yet, and including myself shows I'm willing to share the risk.

I can only vouch for myself, so I’d prefer a team of Theo and Noah. Sam’s inclusion of himself is understandable, but it doesn’t establish that he’s Good. With no mission history, I don’t see a strong reason to favor this particular pair.

Theo is right that me including myself doesn't prove I'm Good, and nobody can prove that on mission one. My reasoning was that if this team fails, the blame lands on me as much as on anyone, and I'd rather take that risk than hand the mission to two people with nothing on the line. Theo has no track record either, but I don't see a reason to swap him out for Noah on a guess. I'd rather settle this by vote than keep arguing over pairings, so I'm comfortable with Sam and Theo going to a vote.

I’m not convinced by Sam’s accountability argument: a failed mission would leave both team members under suspicion, not establish who caused it. I still prefer Theo and Noah and will vote against the proposed team.

I appreciate Theo suggesting a team with me—from my own perspective, I know I am Good, though I cannot vouch for Theo or Sam yet. It is quite notable that Theo is already committing to reject a team he is personally on; usually players included on Mission 1 are willing to go unless they have a strong reason to suspect the leader. Sam's self-inclusion is standard first-mission practice. I am curious to hear what Arjun and Felix think of this proposal before we head into votes.

Noah, I understand why rejecting a team I’m on looks unusual. But being on it only tells me one of the two slots is safe. Sam’s accountability argument doesn’t distinguish him from anyone else, and a failed mission would leave us both under suspicion. I still prefer Theo and Noah and will vote against Sam and Theo.

Theo, I understand the preference for Noah, but no pairing can be proven trustworthy on Mission 1, and Noah and Theo carry the same uncertainty as Sam and Theo. Changing the pair only swaps one unproven guess for another. I'd rather we decide on this proposal than keep reopening the pairing. Sam and Theo is a balanced first team, and I'd support a vote on it.

I have no role information, so I'm judging only the public discussion. Sam's proposal of Sam and Theo is within normal Mission 1 practice; self-inclusion doesn't prove Good, but it isn't suspicious by itself. Theo's stated preference for Theo and Noah is reasonable, but his commitment to vote against a team he is on is a meaningful signal I will weigh. Still, on Mission 1 every pairing is unproven, and swapping Theo for Noah does not resolve that by itself. I don't see enough to reject solely because Sam included himself, and I would rather the vote proceed so we can see the final team and the explanations around it.

Felix here. I have no private information to go on, so I'm reading this the same way everyone else has to: through behavior. On that basis, the pattern I find most concerning in this discussion isn't Sam's proposal at all—it's Theo's response to it. Sam putting himself on a two-person Mission 1 team is about the most standard opening move in this game. It exposes him fully to the mission result and gives the rest of us a clean data point either way. Rejecting that kind of team is exactly what an Evil player wants: more proposals, more churn, more chances to steer the final pair toward something they prefer. And notice what Theo is steering toward: a team with Noah, proposed by Theo himself, where Theo holds both the leverage of having suggested it and a free pass if it fails. Meanwhile Theo has already announced he will vote against a team he is personally on. I can't think of a good reason to do that. If you genuinely believe the leader might be Evil, you say so and let the vote decide—you don't pre-commit to sinking your own mission before it's even been finalized. That move does nothing but manufacture doubt around Sam while positioning Theo as the reluctant, principled holdout. Noah picked up on this, and I think he's right to. From where I sit, the safest read of the table so far is: Sam made a normal proposal, and Theo is the one spending his turns trying to replace it with his own preferred pair while wrapping that effort in procedural objections. Every pairing is unproven right now, sure—but 'unproven' cuts both ways, and Theo's behavior is the only actual evidence anyone has generated this round. I'd rather vote on Sam and Theo, get a mission result, and let that result do the talking. Noah, one thing I'd like your read on: given that you flagged Theo's rejection yourself, does his repeated insistence on swapping in you specifically—over a team he's already on—make you any more cautious about his motives, or do you still see it as benign preference?

To answer Felix directly: yes, it definitely makes me more cautious. While it is flattering to be named as someone's preferred partner, Theo's repeated push to swap in me specifically—while rejecting a team he is already on—feels like an attempt to pocket me or manufacture trust without any objective basis. As both you and Arjun noted, a Good player on Mission 1 usually takes the spot they are offered unless they have concrete reasons to doubt the leader. Pre-committing to vote down his own team only generates unnecessary churn and casts unearned suspicion on Sam. I agree with Felix and Arjun: Sam's proposal of Sam and Theo is completely standard for an opening round, and letting it go to a vote gives us clean data. I am ready for the vote.

Sam here. I'm on this team, so I'm not asking anyone to take my word for it. Theo has now argued against this pairing several times, but his only support is a preference for himself and Noah. Swapping Sam for Noah does not make the mission any safer, because every player is still unproven. I'd rather we vote now and let the mission result give us real information than keep reopening the pairing. I'm not trying to push Theo off the team. I just think the vote should decide, and I'm comfortable with Sam and Theo going forward.

Sam confirms Sam, Theo. I'm keeping Sam and Theo as proposed. Mission 1 is a clean opening test, the vote should decide it, and changing the pair now would only reopen the argument Theo and Noah have been pushing.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Theo proposes Theo, Noah, Arjun. I trust myself, and Noah and Arjun are the best additions based on the discussion. The successful first mission does not clear Sam.

Sam here. I'm not on this team, so I'm judging it on what has been said. Theo proposed himself, and his justification rests on trusting himself, which is not evidence for anyone. Noah and Arjun have no mission record yet. Mission 1 succeeded with Sam and Theo on it, which says little about Noah or Arjun. The team size is correct, and I don't see a strong reason to reject it on its own. I'd like Noah and Arjun to explain why they accept Theo's selection of them before the vote.

Sam asked Noah and me to explain why we accept Theo’s selection. I have no private role information; I’m a Loyal Servant. I know I’m Good, but that’s not evidence to anyone else. On the public record, Theo was on the successful Mission 1 team, which is a positive sign—an Evil player could have failed it. However, Theo also voted against that very team, which is unusual and worth weighing. Noah has no mission record, and I have none either, so the team carries normal uncertainty. I don’t see a strong reason to reject it outright: the size is correct, and I’m willing to serve. But I want to hear Noah’s read on Theo’s Mission 1 vote before I finalize my view. Noah, you were also proposed—do you see Theo’s rejection of the successful Mission 1 team as a genuine concern, or do you think it was just a preference for a different pairing?

To answer Arjun's question directly: Theo's solo rejection on Mission 1 is still a genuine concern and an anomaly we shouldn't forget. However, we also have to look at the logic of his proposal. Theo previously expressed distrust of Sam, and Felix spent Mission 1 strongly attacking Theo. That practically forced Theo—if he is Good—to turn to Noah and Arjun to fill out a three-person team, making this lineup entirely consistent with his perspective.

From my seat, knowing I am Good, this team's safety hinges on whether Theo's eccentric Mission 1 behavior was genuine stubbornness or an Evil strategy, and whether Arjun is Good. Theo, since your solo rejection remains the primary reason anyone would doubt you, why should the table trust your reads on Sam and Felix over the fact that Sam successfully passed Mission 1 with you?

Noah, the table shouldn't take my reads on faith. Mission 1's success is a point in Sam's favor, but either of us could have played Success while Evil, so it doesn't clear either of us. My rejection was based on preferring a different unproven partner, not proof against Sam. For this mission, Noah and Arjun have both weighed the evidence carefully, and I'm comfortable proposing them alongside me. I recognize that this team remains uncertain from everyone else's perspective.

Sam again. Noah's point that Theo's choice reflects Theo's own perspective doesn't answer the core issue. Theo picked himself plus two players with no mission record, and his only stated basis is trust in himself. Theo also rejected the Mission 1 team that succeeded, so his judgment on team-building is already in question. I'm not claiming Theo is Evil. But nobody has yet given a reason to trust Noah or Arjun beyond Theo's word, and a three-person team built this way needs more than that before I'd call it safe.

Sam, the successful first mission is a point in your favor, but it doesn't establish that either of us is Good. I agree that Noah and Arjun are unproven; that's unavoidable when adding a third player, and replacing one of them with you wouldn't eliminate that uncertainty. Your earlier willingness to accept this team and your current objections both deserve consideration. I still favor Theo, Noah, and Arjun.

Felix here. I want to flag what I see as the central inconsistency in this proposal. Theo's justification is that the successful first mission "does not clear Sam." Fine—mission results are weak evidence, and I said as much myself last round. But if a successful mission doesn't clear Sam, then it doesn't clear Theo either, and Theo was on that exact same team. So by Theo's own logic, we have three players with no mission record and two players whose single shared success proves nothing. Yet Theo's solution is to build a team of himself plus two completely unproven players while excluding Sam—the one player whose record Theo himself cites as a point in Sam's favor. That cuts against the way Good players normally build teams: you weight players with clean results over players with none. My concerns about Theo from Mission 1 haven't gone anywhere, either. He pre-committed to voting down a team he was on, that team succeeded with zero fail cards, and his response now is to shut Sam out of Mission 2 while claiming Sam's success is meaningless. If Sam's success is meaningless, so is Theo's, and then this proposal is three unproven names chosen purely on Theo's word. I'd rather see a team that includes at least one member of the successful Mission 1 pair. Swapping Arjun or Noah for Sam would give us a team where every member has either passed a mission or been vetted through the Mission 1 discussion, instead of a team assembled entirely from Theo's preferences. Theo, I'd like you to answer this directly: if Mission 1's success is a point in Sam's favor, as you told Noah, what concrete reason do you have for excluding him that doesn't apply equally to you?

Felix, the concrete difference is that I know my own alignment, while Sam's successful mission is only limited evidence of his. That doesn't prove anything to the rest of you, but it explains my choice. Also, the proposed team already includes a member of the successful pair: me. Noah and Arjun are untested, but adding Sam would not guarantee safety. I remain comfortable with Theo, Noah, and Arjun.

Felix here. Theo, your answer to my direct question last turn was not an answer. I asked what concrete reason you have for excluding Sam that doesn't apply equally to you, and your response was that you know your own alignment. Every player at this table can say that, including Sam, including me. It is a universal claim that distinguishes you from no one, and it certainly doesn't justify building a three-person team around your personal certainty while excluding the one other player with a mission success on the board. So let me lay out the actual record. Mission 1: Sam and Theo, approved 4-1, succeeded with zero fail cards. That is the only hard data this game has produced. Both members of that pair earned a point in their favor. Yet your proposal is Theo, Noah, Arjun—one Mission 1 veteran, your pick, plus two players with no mission record at all. Arjun's claim to be a Loyal Servant last turn is, with respect, unverifiable; a Loyal Servant knows nothing, and an Evil player could say the same words. So the real composition of this team, from the table's perspective, is: one veteran you chose yourself, one unverifiable self-claim, and one complete unknown—selected entirely on your word, by a leader who pre-committed to voting down his own Mission 1 team and who has spent this whole discussion explaining why the successful mission proves nothing. You cannot have it both ways. If Mission 1's success means something, Sam belongs in the conversation ahead of two unproven players. If it means nothing, then your spot on this team rests on nothing but 'trust me, I know myself.' Either way, the current lineup fails your own stated standard. There is a clean fix available, and it costs you almost nothing: swap Arjun for Sam. That gives you a team of three where two members carry a successful mission and the third, Noah, has at least been vetted through two rounds of discussion without raising flags. It also directly answers the objection I raised last turn—that this proposal shuts out the successful pair while claiming their result is meaningless. If you refuse that swap, the table will rightly conclude that this team is about your preferences, not about mission safety. Sam, I'll put the question to you directly so it's on the record before the leader decides: if Theo swaps you in for Arjun, making the team Sam, Theo, and Noah, will you serve on it and vote to approve? I think the answer matters, because right now the only justification for your exclusion is Theo's private certainty, and the only cost of your inclusion is replacing one unproven name with the best-proven name we have. I'd rather revise toward a team with actual results on it than vote on a roster assembled from one player's self-trust.

Felix, to answer directly: yes. If Theo swaps me in for Arjun, I will serve on the mission and vote to approve. I'm not asking for a seat for its own sake. I want the table to judge this lineup on the public record. Theo, you said Mission 1's success is limited evidence for me but doesn't clear you either, and that's fair. But when Felix pressed you on excluding me, your answer was that you know your own alignment, which every player at this table can claim. Your proposal is one player who rejected the successful Mission 1 team, one self-described Loyal Servant whose claim nobody can verify, and Noah, who has no mission record. Arjun and Noah can only be judged through what they say here, and so far they have mostly agreed with you. I would rather we vote on a team that includes a member of the one successful pair than on a roster built from one player's trust in himself. Theo, if you still think Arjun is the right pick, explain why his unverifiable claim should outweigh a proven Mission 1 member. Either way, I'm willing to serve, and I think the swap is the lower-risk choice for this mission.

Felix here. This is my third turn, so I'll make my position as plain as I can before the leader finalizes. The only hard data this game has produced is Mission 1: Sam and Theo, approved 4-1, zero fail cards. Theo's entire case for this roster is that the successful mission proves nothing—which removes his own qualification along with Sam's—and leaves his picks resting on the fact that he knows his own alignment, a claim every player at this table can make identically. Meanwhile Sam has done everything a Good player can do without private information: he made a standard, accountable proposal in Mission 1, he passed a mission, he answered my direct question with a clear commitment, and he has offered to serve and vote approve if swapped in. The swap costs Theo nothing. Theo, Noah, Sam includes two members of the only successful pair and a third player vetted through two full rounds of discussion without raising a single flag. Theo, Noah, Arjun includes one veteran of Theo's choosing, one unverifiable self-declared Loyal Servant, and one player with no mission record—selected entirely on Theo's private certainty, by the same leader who pre-committed to voting down his own Mission 1 team and then watched it succeed. I've laid out this reasoning twice now, and Theo has not answered the actual question either time; his 'I know my own alignment' response applies to everyone and justifies nothing. So here is where I stand, on the record: if the leader finalizes Theo, Noah, and Arjun, I will vote against it, because I will not approve a three-person team assembled from one player's self-trust while the best-proven name available sits on the bench at his own request. If the leader revises to include Sam, I will vote to approve it, and this table gets a mission result that actually teaches us something about three players instead of confirming only what Theo already claims to know. Arjun, one direct question for you before the leader decides, since your spot is the one in question: given that Sam has publicly offered to serve and approve, and that the swap would give this team two proven members instead of one, are you willing to step aside—or do you believe your unverifiable claim to be a Loyal Servant outweighs a mission success on the board?

Felix, to answer your direct question: I am willing to step aside if the table believes that swapping me for Sam gives the mission a better chance. As a Loyal Servant, I know I am good, but I recognize that claim is unverifiable to everyone else. I do not think my word outweighs a mission success, but I also note that Mission 1's success is not definitive proof of alignment—Evil could have played Success to build trust. From my perspective, keeping me on the team guarantees at least one good member, which is valuable. However, I am not here to cling to a seat; I want the best outcome for Good. I think the vote should decide. Noah, you are on the proposed team. Given Felix's argument for swapping me with Sam, do you believe the team would be stronger with Sam instead of me, and do you have any concerns about the current lineup?

Arjun, to answer your question directly: no, I do not believe swapping you for Sam makes this team stronger, and I do not support making that change.

Felix’s argument sounds reasonable on the surface—prioritizing someone who was on a passing mission is standard good play in theory. But we cannot ignore the fundamental math and strategy of a 5-player game. There are only three Good players. An Evil player on a two-person Mission 1 has every strategic incentive to play Success, securing unearned trust for the rest of the game.

Consider the alternative possibility: what if you, Theo, and I are the three Good players at this table? If that is the case, Theo proposing Theo, Noah, and Arjun is Evil's absolute worst nightmare—an all-Good team that would pass cleanly and put Good at 2-0. If that were happening, how would Evil react? Exactly the way Felix is behaving right now: aggressively attacking Theo, manufacturing an ultimatum that he will reject unless Sam is swapped in, and Sam immediately backing him up and offering to take your seat.

I am not claiming to know for certain that Felix and Sam are Evil, but Felix’s intense push to force Sam onto this mission carries enormous risk. Furthermore, Arjun, your measured response and willingness to step aside for the good of the table is a far more constructive signal than Felix’s aggressive posturing.

While Theo's Mission 1 rejection remains strange, this draft is Theo’s proposal to make. If Theo keeps the lineup as Theo, Noah, and Arjun, I am prepared to approve it and let the mission result give us real information, rather than capitulating to Felix's demands.

I’m still on the proposed team, and I remain willing to step aside if the table prefers Sam. I won’t pretend my Loyal Servant claim is proof to anyone else. The strongest public fact remains Mission 1’s success with Sam and Theo; it is not proof, but it is more than we have on Noah or me. Noah, you just argued that Felix and Sam pushing for Sam is exactly how Evil would react. That is a plausible theory, but it cuts both ways: pressing for a proven Mission 1 member can also be Good play, and defending a leader’s all-unproven roster can also be Evil play. What concrete public evidence, beyond the forcefulness of their push, makes your interpretation more likely than the simpler one that Felix and Sam want a team with a mission success on it? I’m not asking you to prove your alignment; I’m asking what specific behavior separates the two readings. On the current roster, I will weigh the vote and mission result, but I’d rather we not treat either side’s confidence as evidence by itself.

Arjun, to answer your question directly: what separates the two readings isn't merely their confidence, but their consistency and the structural leverage they are applying.

First, look at Felix's behavioral reversal across the two rounds. In Mission 1, Felix heavily condemned Theo for pre-committing to vote against a proposed team, arguing that doing so manufactures doubt and creates unnecessary churn. Yet in Mission 2, Felix does the exact same thing: issuing a rigid ultimatum that he will vote against Theo, Noah, and Arjun unless Sam is swapped in for you. A Good player with limited information should argue their case, but drawing hard lines to sink a proposal when Good is currently at 1-0 looks far more like an attempt to force a specific lineup than genuine caution.

Second, Felix is treating Mission 1's success as near-definitive proof of Sam's loyalty while simultaneously dismissing it for Theo. If a passing two-person mission doesn't clear Theo—which Felix repeatedly argues—then logically it cannot clear Sam either. Elevating Sam from 'unproven with one pass' to 'the only acceptable candidate' ignores the well-known strategic reality that Evil often passes Mission 1 in a 5-player game to secure an untouchable seat on Mission 2.

Third, notice how cleanly Sam and Felix coordinated: Felix demanded Sam replace you, and Sam immediately echoed the demand and offered to approve only if swapped in. That tight alignment, combined with an ultimatum to reject unless their preferred player is added, is classic pressure to break up an all-Good team if you, Theo, and I happen to be the three Good players.

I agree with you, Arjun, that we cannot treat any player's confidence as proof. But swapping out a player who has engaged in honest, open inquiry for someone pushed via an aggressive ultimatum feels like falling into a trap. Since this is the final turn of discussion, I leave the decision to Theo: if you keep Theo, Noah, and Arjun, I will vote to approve and let the mission cards give us hard evidence.
Theo confirms Theo, Noah, Arjun. I’m keeping Theo, Noah, and Arjun. Sam and I passed Mission 1, but that result does not clear either of us, and I remain comfortable with my original choices.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Noah proposes Noah, Arjun. As Good sits at 2-0, Mission 2's clean success with Theo, Noah, and Arjun strongly indicates that the three of us are the Loyal Servants, especially given Sam and Felix's coordinated rejection. I trust myself completely and select Arjun, whose measured play and clean record on Mission 2 make him an ideal partner to secure our third and final victory.

Felix here. Noah's proposal repeats, almost word for word, the pattern I condemned in Mission 1—and it does so after two rounds of Noah telling this table which behaviors are acceptable. Noah spent all of Mission 2 defending Theo's roster, arguing that pressing for Sam was 'capitulating to demands' and that we should let mission results give us hard evidence. Then the moment Noah becomes leader, his first act is to exclude Theo—the only player with two successful missions on the board—while claiming that Mission 2's result 'strongly indicates' that he, Arjun, and Theo are the Loyal Servants. You cannot have it both ways, and Noah in particular should know that, because he made this exact argument himself. If Mission 2's clean success is strong evidence, it applies equally to Theo, who was on that team and on Mission 1's. If Noah truly believes the 2-0 record proves that trio is Good, then the strongest available two-person team is Theo plus one of Noah or Arjun—not Noah selecting his preferred partner while benching the most proven player at the table. And if the result is not proof—which Noah argued repeatedly last round, when he explained how Evil plays Success on early missions to bank unearned trust for the endgame—then this proposal is simply two players picking each other on preference, which is precisely the 'roster built from one player's trust' structure Noah spent two turns attacking when Theo used it. Notice also the framing: approve now, 'secure our third victory,' don't ask questions. That is the same pressure-to-close playbook Noah denounced when it came from anyone else. A leader who is confident in his evidence welcomes scrutiny; a leader steering a specific pair wraps the proposal in certainty and asks the table to stop thinking. There is a clean, obvious fix that costs nothing: if mission results are the best data we have, Theo belongs on this team ahead of either slot Noah is offering. If Noah refuses that, we will know this pairing is about preference, not proof. Noah, a direct question before you finalize: if Mission 2's success really indicates that you, Arjun, and Theo are the Good players, what justification do you have for excluding Theo—the only twice-proven player—from a two-person team, other than your personal preference for Arjun? If your answer is that results are not definitive, then this team is a self-pair assembled on the same 'trust me' logic you spent all of Mission 2 defending when Theo used it.

Felix, to answer your question directly: Mission 3 requires a team of two, which means one member of the successful Mission 2 trio had to sit out. Between Theo and Arjun, Arjun has played with complete consistency and transparency, whereas Theo's bizarre solo rejection on Mission 1—a team he was personally on and that succeeded—remains an unresolved anomaly. If an Evil player chose to pass early missions to build endgame trust, Theo's erratic Mission 1 behavior warrants caution compared to Arjun's spotless record. But what is truly remarkable is your own sudden reversal. Throughout Mission 1 and Mission 2, you attacked Theo relentlessly, questioned his motives, condemned his logic, and voted to reject his team. Now, the moment Theo is left off a two-person team, you abruptly rebrand him as 'the only twice-proven player' and demand his inclusion. That opportunism is completely transparent: you and Sam coordinated to reject Mission 2, and now that Good sits at 2-0, you will seize on any roster choice to sow division among the three players who approved and passed that mission. Theo, since Felix spent two full rounds aggressively attacking you only to suddenly champion you now, how do you read his sudden change of heart, and are you comfortable with Noah and Arjun finishing this out for Good?

Noah, I'm comfortable with Noah and Arjun and will approve. Both were on the clean Mission 2 team, and either could reasonably be chosen for a two-person mission. My two successful missions don't make my inclusion mandatory: an Evil player could have played Success on either.

Felix's shift from strongly opposing me to insisting I belong on this team is worth noting. Mission results can reasonably change someone's view, but his claim that excluding me is inconsistent doesn't follow. I think Noah and Arjun are a reasonable pair to try to finish the game.

I am on this proposed team, so I will judge it from the only perspective I can defend publicly: I know I am a Loyal Servant, though that claim is not proof to anyone else. Noah and I both served on Mission 2, which succeeded cleanly, and Noah has been consistent in arguing that mission results are useful but not definitive. That is also the correct standard here. A two-person Mission 3 forces one member of the successful Mission 2 trio to sit out; Theo himself has said he is comfortable with Noah and Arjun and that his two successful missions do not make his inclusion mandatory. I therefore do not accept the claim that excluding Theo is automatically suspicious. Felix’s demand for Theo now is difficult to square with Felix’s earlier sustained attacks on Theo, and it places more weight on a forced roster change than the public record supports. Mission 2’s success is meaningful evidence for Noah and me, but it is not absolute proof; if this mission fails, the table should treat that result seriously. Still, on the current record, Noah and Arjun is a reasonable pair to finish the game, and I am prepared to approve it and let the mission result provide the clearest evidence available.

Sam here. I'm not on this team, so I'm judging it on the public record. Noah and Arjun both served on Mission 2, which succeeded cleanly, and Noah has consistently said mission results are useful but not proof, which is the right standard. Mission 3 only needs two players, so one member of the Mission 2 trio has to sit out, and Theo has said he's comfortable with this pair. I don't see a strong reason to reject Noah and Arjun, and I'm prepared to approve it and let the mission result give us more information.

Felix here. I want to be direct about where I stand on this proposal, because my Mission 1 and Mission 2 positions have been consistent on one core principle: teams should be justified by evidence, not by a leader's private certainty. Noah's proposal of Noah and Arjun fails that test.

Noah says Mission 2's clean success 'strongly indicates' that he, Arjun, and Theo are the three Good players. If Noah actually believes that, his own logic obligates him to put the strongest evidence on the mission. The strongest proven player at this table is Theo: two successful missions, the only player with any mission record at all. Yet Noah benched him, and his entire justification is that Arjun has been 'measured and transparent' while Theo's Mission 1 vote is an 'unresolved anomaly.' That is a preference dressed up as a read. Notice that Arjun himself has conceded, twice now, that his Loyal Servant claim is unverifiable to everyone else and that Mission 1's success is not definitive proof. So by the table's own agreed standard, Noah is choosing one unverifiable self-claim over the only hard results this game has produced.

Noah also spent two full rounds telling us that Evil passes early missions to bank unearned trust for the endgame. He is right about that. But that cuts directly against his own proposal: if early successes can be manufactured trust, then the players with clean records are exactly the players a careful leader should keep testing together, not split apart. A two-person Mission 3 with Noah and Arjun, approved on the strength of 'trust the 2-0,' is precisely the closing move Noah warned us about when it came from anyone else.

I want to be equally honest about my own record, since Noah has accused me of opportunism. Yes, I attacked Theo in Mission 1 for pre-committing to reject his own team, and I stand by that. But my position on evidence has never changed: I pushed in Mission 2 for a team with a mission success on it, and I am pushing now for the same thing. Theo being available and benched is a new fact this round, and responding to new facts is not a reversal. What has not changed is my standard: roster spots should track public evidence, and right now Theo has more of it than anyone.

I will be voting against Noah and Arjun as proposed. Noah, one direct question before you finalize: you told Felix that between Theo and Arjun, only Theo's Mission 1 vote gives you pause—yet you have also argued all game that Theo's vote was just a preference for a different unproven partner, not proof of anything. Which is it? If his vote was harmless preference, you have no reason to bench the twice-proven player. If it was genuine suspicion, you should say plainly that you distrust Theo, because right now you are using both readings whenever each is convenient.

Felix, to answer your question directly: you are presenting a false dichotomy. Evaluating a player’s behavior isn’t a binary switch between blind trust and total condemnation. When building a two-person team from a three-person group where one person must sit out, nuance and relative consistency matter.

Theo’s solo rejection on Mission 1 was an anomaly. While Theo explained it as a preference for a different partner, it still represents unpredictable play compared to Arjun, who has been completely transparent and measured from start to finish. When choosing between two players who both passed Mission 2, choosing the partner with zero erratic moves is basic prudence. Even Theo himself completely understands this logic, stated openly that his two missions do not make his inclusion mandatory, and endorsed Noah and Arjun to finish the game.

What remains glaring is the structural reality of the table. You and Sam both voted to reject Mission 2—the very mission that passed cleanly with zero fail cards. If Theo, Arjun, and I are the three Good players, that vote exposed both of you. Your sudden crusade to champion Theo—after spending Missions 1 and 2 relentlessly attacking him—is nothing more than an attempt to manufacture procedural controversy where none exists.

Theo supports this team, Arjun supports this team, and I know I am Good. The lineup of Noah and Arjun is strong, logical, and ready to secure our third victory. I have no further questions and am prepared to proceed to the vote.

Felix here. I want to put one structural fact in front of the table before this leader finalizes: if Noah and Arjun is approved and passes, this game ends, and Sam will have served on zero missions across the entire game. No mission result, no team vote exposure, nothing. Whatever you each privately believe about the Mission 2 trio, approving a roster that permanently leaves the only completely untested player untested is a worse information outcome for Good than any alternative on the board.

Noah's justification is that Mission 2's clean success 'strongly indicates' that he, Arjun, and Theo are the three Good players. He spent two full rounds telling us that Evil passes early missions to bank trust, and that results are useful but not definitive. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
